title: A Modified Black-Scholes-Merton Model for Option Pricing
subject: Quantitative Finance
summary: Explains the Black-Scholes-Merton formula for pricing options, where it falls short, and a modified version that fits real markets better.

intro.title: A New Quest
intro.speaker: PROF. QUANT
pages: Welcome, scholar! Today's paper: "A Modified Black-Scholes-Merton Model for Option Pricing".
It is 16 pages long. I turned it into 5 worlds: The Pricing Quest, The Time & Memory Maze, Conformable Time Lab, The Volatility Lab, Market Flex Quest.
An AI helped me explain this paper in plain words. AI can slip up, so check anything important against the paper.
Move with A and D, jump with W. Stomp bears for fun facts, and reach each flag for a lesson. Go!

worlds.name: World 1: The Pricing Quest

cutscenes.title: Pricing Mystery
cutscenes.speaker: PROF. QUANT
pages: Welcome, brave adventurer! Financial derivatives are special contracts whose price depends entirely on another asset, like a company's stock.
Because stock prices jump around in wild and unpredictable ways, figuring out a fair price for these contracts is a tricky puzzle.
The classic math model, known as BSM, tries to solve this puzzle. But it assumes things never change, which causes problems in real life.

practice.prompt: Why is figuring out the price of a financial derivative tricky?
choices: Because the math uses zero numbers
Because markets are always closed
Because contracts have no underlying asset
Because stock prices jump around wildly
practice.explanation: Derivatives depend on underlying stocks, and stock prices move in volatile, unpredictable ways.

cutscenes.title: Fixing Constant Flaws
cutscenes.speaker: PROF. QUANT
pages: The classic BSM model assumes that risk-free interest rates and stock volatility stay totally constant over time.
In reality, risk and interest rates shift constantly! Critics point out this major flaw makes the classic model fail in many real markets.
Some scientists swapped standard randomness for fractional motion to remember past price trends, while others tried iterative procedures.

practice.prompt: What is a major criticism of the classic BSM model?
choices: It ignores the underlying stock entirely
It requires too many physical computers
It assumes interest rates and volatility never change
It only works on weekends
practice.explanation: The classic model relies on the assumption that volatility and risk-free rates are constant over time.

cutscenes.title: The Conformable Upgrade
cutscenes.speaker: PROF. QUANT
pages: Our paper introduces a fresh contender: the conformable BSM model, designed to give us much better flexibility in emerging markets.
We test three contenders side-by-side: classic BSM, long-memory fractional BSM, and our shiny new conformable BSM.

practice.prompt: How did the new conformable BSM perform against the other models?
choices: It failed completely on day one
It performed exactly the same as classic BSM
It was slower than manual calculation
It outperformed them in most scenarios
practice.explanation: The empirical findings show the conformable BSM outperforms the older models in most scenarios.

facts: Financial derivatives change in value based on an underlying security, making their pricing quite tricky.
The classic BSM model assumes that risk-free interest rates and volatility never change.
Fractional motion uses a non-local operator to help models remember past price trends.
Researchers tested three different pricing models side-by-side in a semi-strong efficient market.
The newly proposed conformable BSM model beat the older models in most test scenarios!

questions.prompt: What makes pricing financial derivatives difficult according to our journey?
choices: Computers cannot handle multiplication
Too many regulations closing the markets
The lack of any underlying financial assets
Wild and unpredictable stock price movements
questions.explanation: Derivatives depend on underlying securities that have volatile and unpredictable price movements.

questions.prompt: Which assumption of the classic BSM model is most widely criticized?
choices: That all traders use the exact same computer
Constant volatility and risk-free interest rates
That markets only operate at night
That stock prices always go straight down
questions.explanation: Critics frequently attack the assumption that volatility and risk-free rates stay constant over time.

questions.prompt: What is the main perk of using fractional motion in price dynamics?
choices: It guarantees zero risk for all traders
It completely removes the need for math
It stops the stock market from ever crashing
It models long memory of past price movements
questions.explanation: The non-locality of the fractional operator serves as a tool for modeling long memory in price dynamics.

questions.prompt: How did the authors evaluate the newly proposed conformable BSM model?
choices: Through an empirical comparison with two other models
By ignoring all historical financial data
By guessing prices based on weather patterns
By running a video game simulation
questions.explanation: The paper conducts an empirical comparison of the classic, fractional, and conformable BSM models.

worlds.name: World 2: The Time & Memory Maze

cutscenes.title: Fixing the Classic Formula
cutscenes.speaker: PROF. QUANT
pages: Welcome, students! The classic pricing formula assumes everything stays constant, which is a bit too rigid for real life.
To fix this, smart folks tried letting parameters change smoothly as time moves forward.
This lets our pricing tool adapt to how traders actually expect securities to behave in the wild.

practice.prompt: Why did researchers introduce time-varying parameters into the classic pricing formula?
choices: To make the math much harder
To remove all risk from trading
To match changing market expectations
To speed up computer processing
practice.explanation: Allowing parameters to change with time helps the model capture real-world market behavior and views.

cutscenes.title: The Memory Trap of Fractions
cutscenes.speaker: PROF. QUANT
pages: Next, people tried using fractional math to track long-range dependence, or long memory, in asset prices.
Think of memory like an elephant that remembers every past wiggle, creating slow decay in data.
Sadly, this memory adds a tricky extra parameter and gobbles up computer power like a hungry monster!

practice.prompt: What is a major downside of using fractional derivatives in asset pricing models?
choices: They ignore all past price data
They are too simple to calculate
They always predict zero volatility
They demand heavy computer resources
practice.explanation: Fractional derivatives have non-local memory, making calculations numerically challenging and heavy on resources.

cutscenes.title: Conformable to the Rescue
cutscenes.speaker: PROF. QUANT
pages: Enter conformable derivatives! These clever tools avoid the heavy baggage of long-range memory.
They keep all the nice, simple rules of regular calculus that we already know and love.
That means you get flexibility without burning out your computer trying to calculate past echoes!

practice.prompt: How do conformable derivatives differ from fractional derivatives?
choices: They lack long-range memory
They cannot be computed at all
They require infinite past data
They throw out all calculus rules
practice.explanation: Unlike fractional derivatives, conformable derivatives do not exhibit non-local memory, making them much easier to use.

facts: Classic pricing models assume parameters never change, which is like predicting weather without seasons.
Fractional math gives formulas a long memory, remembering price wiggles from way back when.
Long memory in math sounds cool, but it acts like a nuisance parameter that drains computer power.
Conformable derivatives dodge heavy memory traps while keeping standard calculus rules safe.
Choosing the right math operator can turn a slow, crashing computer model into a smooth runner.

questions.prompt: What was the main goal of adding time-varying coefficients to the traditional pricing model?
choices: To eliminate the need for any equations
To create permanent long-range memory
To drop all security prices to zero
To capture changing market views over time
questions.explanation: Time-varying coefficients let the model reflect how the market views the future behavior of assets.

questions.prompt: Why can fractional Brownian motion cause headaches for financial mathematicians?
choices: It only works for exactly half a day
It introduces a tricky nuisance parameter
It makes all asset returns negative
It completely erases recent price drops
questions.explanation: Long memory introduces a nuisance parameter (H) that makes estimation a much harder task.

questions.prompt: What makes conformable derivatives computationally friendlier than fractional ones?
choices: They ignore time entirely
They rely on non-local past operators
They preserve normal integer-order rules
They use random number generators
questions.explanation: Conformable derivatives keep all rules of integer-order derivatives valid, making computations much simpler.

questions.prompt: If a derivative operator is non-local, what does that mean for calculations?
choices: It assumes prices never fluctuate
It refuses to run on modern computers
It calculates based on values far away
It only looks at values right now
questions.explanation: Non-local operators calculate points based on values far away, creating heavy computational memory needs.

questions.prompt: What is the biggest overall trade-off when picking a derivative type for market pricing?
choices: Printer ink versus screen pixels
Stock volume versus coin weight
Speed versus memory and complexity
Color versus black and white graphs
questions.explanation: You trade off capturing complex memory effects against the heavy computational cost and estimation difficulty.

worlds.name: World 3: Conformable Time Lab
worlds.section: Solving the BSM with Time-Varying Parameters via Conformable Calculus

cutscenes.title: Variable Switch Trick
cutscenes.speaker: PROF. QUANT
pages: Welcome, students! Today we look at a special math trick called the conformable derivative.
Think of it as simply swapping your variables to see the pricing puzzle in a brand new way.
Applying this neat trick to our classic pricing formula helps us unlock fresh insights.

choices: To change variables and gain new insights
To replace the need for computers
To make stock prices go straight up
To completely eliminate market risk
practice.explanation: Just like changing variables in regular math, it gives us a fresh viewpoint on the formula.

cutscenes.title: Time-Varying Gear Shift
cutscenes.speaker: PROF. QUANT
pages: Real markets do not stay still, so our formula needs parameters that change over time.
By plugging our special derivative into the equation, we can tackle these moving targets.
This lets us adapt the classic pricing setup to handle shifting real-world conditions.

practice.prompt: Why do we need time-varying parameters in our pricing equation?
choices: To match the speed of internet trades
It is a rule required by the government
Real financial markets are constantly changing
Because static numbers break calculators
practice.explanation: Markets shift constantly, so our parameters must change over time to keep pace.

cutscenes.title: Short-Term Polynomial Curves
cutscenes.speaker: PROF. QUANT
pages: To make our moving equation actually work, we need a structure for these changing functions.
Real data tests show that order-two polynomials fit short-term trends very well.
These curved shapes capture how volatility and interest rates move in the near future.

practice.prompt: What mathematical shape works best to represent short-term rates and volatility?
choices: Order-two polynomials
Random scatter plots
Perfect straight lines
Static constant numbers
practice.explanation: Data suggests order-two polynomials are quite suitable for short-term rate and volatility.

facts: A conformable derivative acts just like a clever variable swap in classic calculus.
Real markets change constantly, so our math parameters must also shift over time.
Order-two polynomials help us map out short-term market behavior accurately.
Classic pricing formulas often struggle when applied directly to emerging markets.
Testing our new theoretical models with real data bridges math and reality.

choices: It removes all risk from options

It replaces calculus entirely

questions.explanation: The text notes that the conformable derivative can be seen as a change of variables.

questions.prompt: What specific shape is suggested by empirical analysis for short-term parameters?
choices: Order-two polynomials

Exponential decay loops
A single flat line
questions.explanation: An empirical analysis suggests order-two polynomials are suitable for short-term functions.

worlds.name: World 4: The Volatility Lab

cutscenes.title: Checking for Jumpy Prices
cutscenes.speaker: PROF. QUANT
pages: Financial markets often show 'ARCH effects,' which is just a fancy way of saying price jumps tend to cluster together.
We use the Lagrange multiplier test to confirm if these clusters exist before we start building our math model.
Think of it like checking if a road is bumpy before deciding how fast you can drive your car safely.

practice.prompt: Why do we test for ARCH effects before modeling prices?
choices: To calculate the total share count
To see if the market is closed
To detect clusters of price volatility
To find the cheapest stock available
practice.explanation: Testing for ARCH effects helps us understand if volatility comes in waves, which is crucial for accurate predictions.

cutscenes.title: Smoothing Out the Curves
cutscenes.speaker: PROF. QUANT
pages: Market data is messy, so we use a quadratic regression to draw a smooth curve through the noisy volatility points.
This turns unpredictable data into a clean, flexible math equation we can actually solve.
It acts like a filter, stripping away random background noise to show the true trend beneath.

practice.prompt: What is the main purpose of using a quadratic regression on volatility data?
choices: To increase the speed of the computer
To eliminate all future market risk
To make the data look more colorful
To create a smooth trend from noisy data
practice.explanation: Regression helps us fit a clean curve to data points, making it easier to use in our pricing model.

cutscenes.title: The Conformal Advantage
cutscenes.speaker: PROF. QUANT
pages: Our new model, the 'Conformal' approach, adapts better to emerging markets than the classic, rigid BSM formula.
By comparing it against older models, we see it consistently produces smaller errors across different time lengths.
It is like upgrading from a fixed-gear bike to one with gears that shift perfectly for any hill.

practice.prompt: How does the conformal model perform compared to the classic BSM?
choices: It only works on government bonds
It is much slower at calculating
It consistently has smaller errors
It has larger errors in all tests
practice.explanation: The study shows the conformal model is more accurate, leading to smaller pricing errors than the traditional BSM.

facts: The model uses 28-day treasury bond yields as a stand-in for the risk-free interest rate.
Even when models look different on paper, their variance estimates can end up being identical.
Higher maturity dates for options actually lead to less messy, more stable estimates.
Market efficiency doesn't stop price clusters from appearing in the data.
The conformal model rarely gets beaten by the classic BSM or fractional models.

worlds.name: World 5: Market Flex Quest

cutscenes.title: Why Old Models Falter
cutscenes.speaker: PROF. QUANT
pages: Traditional pricing tools assume markets are perfect and mature.
In places like Mexico, companies often have managers who act like owners.
This lack of separation makes standard math formulas fail to track prices well.

practice.prompt: Why do standard models struggle in emerging markets?
choices: Not enough traders
Computers are too slow
Lack of manager-stockholder split
Too many public firms
practice.explanation: When managers and owners are the same, the market behaves differently than the traditional model expects.

cutscenes.title: The Conformable Tweak
cutscenes.speaker: PROF. QUANT
pages: We use something called conformable calculus to add flexibility.
Think of it as adding a 'wiggle room' knob to the old math formula.
This knob lets our model adapt to the unique quirks of developing markets.

practice.prompt: What is the role of the conformable parameter?
choices: To reduce transaction costs
To speed up trading platforms
To adjust the model for market quirks
To predict future stock crashes
practice.explanation: The parameter acts like a knob to fine-tune the model, making it more flexible for specific market conditions.

cutscenes.title: Winning the Accuracy Race
cutscenes.speaker: PROF. QUANT
pages: Our new model was tested against older ones in many different scenarios.
It provided the best results in over 90% of our test cases.
While promising, we still need more data to prove it works everywhere.

choices: It was best in over 90% of cases

It only worked on weekends

facts: Our model hit the bullseye in over 90% of tested market scenarios.
A 'conformable parameter' near 0.8 seems to be the sweet spot for these calculations.
In Mexico, nearly 72% of firms don't clearly separate managers from owners.
This is the first study to apply this math to real-world financial data.
We used public data from Yahoo Finance and Bloomberg terminals for our research.
